At ten, Kishore got stuck on the word "temperature" while reading aloud. His face went hot. He stuck out his tongue, wobbled his head and read the next line like a robot. The class burst into laughter, and Kishore bowed, but his hands shook on the book.
At twenty, Kishore sat at the back of a presentation. Anjali, at the front, said "1950" when she meant "1590" and did not notice. Kishore let out a low, quiet chortle, a private little sound. Anjali heard it. Her cheeks burned, and she stopped in the middle of a sentence. Afterwards, she said to her friend Himani, "He laughed at my mistake." Himani frowned. "Maybe ask him what it meant?" Anjali found Kishore outside. "Were you laughing at me?" Kishore blinked. "No, sorry, it was relief. I made the same slip in my presentation last week, and thought I was the only one. I should have kept quiet." Anjali let out a breath. "It sounded like mocking." He nodded. "I'll be careful how I laugh," he said.

qa.q: What number did Anjali say instead of "1590"?
How do the laughter at ten and the chortle at twenty show that the same sound can mean different things?
qa.a: At ten Kishore made the class laugh with him, and it covered his shaking hands. At twenty his quiet chortle was relief, but aimed at Anjali's slip it sounded like mocking, so context decides what a laugh means.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling when she stopped mid-sentence and her cheeks burned?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and hurt, thinking that Kishore was laughing at her mistake.

qa.q: What did Himani do well, and what could Kishore do next time?
qa.a: Himani suggested asking what it meant instead of assuming. Kishore can keep quiet or say something kind when someone slips, so his sound is not read as mockery.

grounding: A class clown's joke covering embarrassment (3891) and, years later, a private chortle at someone's slip that could be read as mockery though it was relief (2682).
